tests.statement: Γ = the division hull of ℤP has rank 1 but is not finitely generated; Γ_ℝ is still one-dimensional: finite rank, not finite generation, is the hypothesis.

nodes.title: The constants c_NT and h₁ of an embedded abelian variety
nodes.statement: Let A ⊆ ℙⁿ be an abelian variety over ℚ̄ embedded projectively normally by a basis ξ₀, …, ξ_n of H⁰(A, L) for a symmetric very ample L. Then c_NT(A) ≥ 0 is the least constant with |ĥ_L − h| ≤ c_NT on A(ℚ̄), and h₁(A) is the height of the coefficient vector for a chosen family of bihomogeneous polynomials P_{ij} of bidegree (2, 2) with f^*(p₁^*ξ_i ⊗ p₂^*ξ_j) = P_{ij}(p₁^*ξ, p₂^*ξ) for f(P, Q) = (P + Q, P − Q).
hypotheses: A ⊆ ℙⁿ projectively normal by a symmetric very ample L.
proofSteps: c_NT exists by the height machine (Tate’s limit, parent RP.0).
The polynomials P_{ij} exist since f^*(L ⊠ L) ≅ L² ⊠ L² (theorem of the cube) and projective normality makes the multiplication maps on sections surjective (Rémond, Proposition 5.2, cited by DGH).

sources.match: Defines the constant bounding the difference between the Néron–Tate and naive heights and the height of the addition-and-subtraction polynomials of bidegree (2, 2), whose existence it takes from Rémond.
Uses the same two constants in the David–Philippon formulation of Rémond’s theorem.

acceptance: For an elliptic curve in ℙ² by the Weierstrass embedding (L = O(3·O)), c_NT is bounded by an explicit multiple of max{1, h(j)} plus the height of the Weierstrass coefficients (Silverman’s difference bounds).
c_NT ≥ 0 and h₁ ≥ 0.

Projective normality supplies the needed surjections on sections. Symmetric ample bundles which are not powers M^{⊗k}, k ≥ 3, can still be projectively normal (for example O_E(4·0)); being such a power is sufficient, not a necessary condition.

uses.how: Rémond’s large-point bound depends on max{1, h(C), c_NT, h₁}
the counting of Theorem 7.1 is stated in terms of c_NT and h₁

api.name: EmbeddingConstants.cNT
api.statement: c_NT(A) for the embedding.

api.name: EmbeddingConstants.h1
api.statement: h₁(A; (P_{ij})) is the absolute logarithmic height of the projective coefficient vector of a chosen addition/difference polynomial family.

api.name: EmbeddingConstants.abs_sub_le
api.statement: |ĥ_L(P) − h(P)| ≤ c_NT(A) for all P ∈ A(ℚ̄).

api.name: EmbeddingConstants.galois
api.statement: c_NT and h₁ are unchanged by simultaneously conjugating A, its embedding, and the chosen polynomial family.

tests.name: EmbeddingConstants.elliptic_x
tests.statement: For an elliptic curve in ℙ² by the Weierstrass embedding (L = O(3·O)), c_NT is bounded by an explicit multiple of max{1, h(j)} plus the height of the Weierstrass coefficients (Silverman’s difference bounds).

tests.name: EmbeddingConstants.nonneg
tests.statement: c_NT ≥ 0 and h₁ ≥ 0.

tests.name: EmbeddingConstants.not_projectively_normal
tests.statement: Projective normality supplies the needed surjections on sections. Symmetric ample bundles which are not powers M^{⊗k}, k ≥ 3, can still be projectively normal (for example O_E(4·0)); being such a power is sufficient, not a necessary condition.

nodes.title: Bounds for c_NT and h₁ by the Faltings height (DGH (8.4), (8.7))
nodes.statement: Fix g, a projective embedding of the level-ℓ universal principally polarized family as in DGH §6.1, and the power l used there. For its fibre embeddings there is c′ depending on these fixed choices such that c_NT(A) ≤ c′ max{1,h_{A_g,M}([A])}, and one can choose addition/difference polynomials with h₁(A) ≤ c′ max{1,h_{A_g,M}([A])}. Thus both are bounded by c″ max{1,h_Fal(A)}. The embedding and polynomial family are controlled choices; arbitrary changes of projective coordinates are excluded. The extension to general polarization types used in GGK Appendix A is a separate input recorded as a gap.
hypotheses: A principally polarized of dimension g with the fixed universal-family embedding and chosen controlled polynomial family of DGH §6.1 and §8.
proofSteps: c_NT: Silverman–Tate in the universal family (parent RP.0): |ĥ(P) − h(P)| ≤ c max{1, h(π(P))}.

h₁: the coefficients of the P_{ij} solve a linear system whose equations are evaluations at finitely many torsion points (Zariski dense, of height zero); Cramer’s rule bounds their height linearly in the height of the moduli point.
Convert the moduli height into max{1, h_Fal(A)} by the comparison of ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeights R35.5.

sources.locator: Proof of Proposition 8.1, (8.4) and (8.6)–(8.7), pp. 32–33 (arXiv v3)
sources.match: Bounds c_NT by Silverman–Tate in the universal family and obtains the addition polynomials with controlled height by Cramer’s rule from a linear system at finitely many torsion points.
Records both constants as bounded by a constant depending on g and deg_L A times max{1, h_Fal(A)}.

acceptance: Both bounds are linear in max{1, h_Fal(A)}, which is what makes the threshold of the gap principle the right scale for Rémond’s large points.

nodes.title: Rémond’s generalized Vojta inequality
nodes.statement: Let A be an abelian variety over ℚ̄ with L symmetric, very ample and projectively normal, n = deg_L A/g! − 1, and X ⊆ A irreducible. There are c₄, c₅ > 0 depending on g, deg_L X and deg_L A such that if P₀, …, P_{dim X} ∈ X°(ℚ̄) satisfy ⟨P_i, P_{i+1}⟩ ≥ (1 − 1/c₄)|P_i||P_{i+1}| and |P_{i+1}| ≥ c₄|P_i| for all i, then |P₀|² ≤ c₅ max{1, h(X), h_Fal(A)}. The Faltings-height form assumes the controlled-embedding bound in the hypotheses; for an arbitrary embedding its right side instead uses max{1,h(X),c_NT,h₁}.
hypotheses: L symmetric very ample projectively normal; X irreducible; P_i ∈ X° in a narrow cone with rapidly increasing norms.

For the displayed Faltings-height form, require a controlled embedding and a polynomial family with max{c_NT,h₁} ≤ C(g,deg_L A) max{1,h_Fal(A)}. Without that input, retain max{1,h(X),c_NT,h₁} in the bound.
proofSteps: Rémond’s explicit values (Théorème 1.1): with m = dim X + 1, c₁ = c₂ = max(deg X, (6m)^{2m})^{m^{3m²}} and c₃ = c₁(n + 1)^{(dim X)³} max(h(X), h₁, c_NT, n log(n + 1)); here the first point need only satisfy |x₁|² ≥ c₃ for some x_i to lie in Z_X. This is Rémond’s quantitative form of the Faltings–Vojta inequality: the parent plans the qualitative higher-dimensional Vojta method (RP.5, Faltings’ product theorem, small sections and dimension descent); Rémond’s version tracks every constant through the same construction in terms of n, deg X, h(X), c_NT and h₁.

First retain the bound in max{1,h(X),c_NT,h₁} for the chosen embedding. Only under the additional controlled-embedding hypothesis replace c_NT,h₁ by C(g,deg_L A) max{1,h_Fal(A)}. DGH proves this input for its fixed principally polarized family; the general-polarization input remains a gap.

sources.locator: Theorem A.1, p. 227 (citing Rémond, Inégalité de Vojta en dimension supérieure, Theorem 1.1)
sources.match: Restates Rémond’s explicit Vojta inequality for points of the complement of the Ueno locus with growing norms in a narrow cone, with constants depending only on g and the degrees and the dependence on h(X) and h_Fal(A) explicit.

sources.locator: Théorème 1.1, p. 105, and Théorème 1.2, p. 106; setting §1, p. 104
sources.match: For a geometrically integral X in a projectively normal symmetric embedding of A over a number field, shows that dim X + 1 points of X off the union Z_X of translates of positive-dimensional abelian subvarieties cannot be pairwise at small angle, of rapidly increasing norm and of large first norm, with explicit constants in deg X, n, h(X), c_NT and h₁.

acceptance: The constants do not depend on A, X or the points beyond the listed degrees and heights.
For X a curve of genus ≥ 2 in its Jacobian this is Bombieri’s explicit Vojta inequality with an explicit dependence on the height of the curve.
The cone condition is essential: without small angles there is no inequality (two orthogonal points can have arbitrary norms).

nodes.title: Rémond’s generalized Mumford inequality
nodes.statement: With A, L, n and X as in Rémond’s Vojta inequality, let D_{dim X} : X^{dim X+1} → A^{dim X}, (x₀, …, x_{dim X}) ↦ (x₁ − x₀, …, x_{dim X} − x₀). There are c₄, c₅ > 0 depending on g, deg_L X and deg_L A such that if P₀, …, P_{dim X} ∈ X(ℚ̄) with (P₀, …, P_{dim X}) isolated in its fibre of D_{dim X}, ⟨P₀, P_i⟩ ≥ (1 − 1/c₄)|P₀||P_i| and ||P₀| − |P_i|| ≤ |P₀|/c₄ for all i, then |P₀|² ≤ c₅ max{1, h(X), h_Fal(A)}. The Faltings-height form assumes the controlled-embedding bound in the hypotheses; for an arbitrary embedding its right side instead uses max{1,h(X),c_NT,h₁}.
hypotheses: as in Rémond’s Vojta inequality; the tuple isolated in its D_{dim X}-fibre.

For the displayed Faltings-height form, require a controlled embedding and a polynomial family with max{c_NT,h₁} ≤ C(g,deg_L A) max{1,h_Fal(A)}. Without that input, retain max{1,h(X),c_NT,h₁} in the bound.
proofSteps: Generalizes Mumford’s gap principle for curves (parent RP.5): an arithmetic Bézout estimate for the height of an isolated point of the fibre of D_{dim X} against the heights of the coordinates, with the quadratic terms controlled by the angle and norm conditions.

First retain the bound in max{1,h(X),c_NT,h₁} for the chosen embedding. Only under the additional controlled-embedding hypothesis replace c_NT,h₁ by C(g,deg_L A) max{1,h_Fal(A)}. DGH proves this input for its fixed principally polarized family; the general-polarization input remains a gap.

sources.locator: Proposition A.2, p. 228 (citing Rémond, Décompte dans une conjecture de Lang, Proposition 3.4)
sources.match: Restates Rémond’s generalized Mumford inequality: isolated tuples of points of nearly equal norm in a narrow cone have bounded norm, explicitly in the degrees and heights.

acceptance: For dim X = 1 this is Mumford’s gap principle for curves with explicit constants.
Isolation is necessary: if the fibre is positive-dimensional the tuple can be moved along a coset and no bound holds.

nodes.title: Isolated fibres or a small exceptional set (GGK Proposition A.3)
nodes.statement: With X ⊆ A irreducible and D_{dim X} as in Rémond’s Mumford inequality, every Ξ ⊆ X°(ℚ̄) satisfies one of: (i) for every x ∈ X(ℚ̄) there are pairwise distinct x₁, …, x_{dim X} ∈ Ξ with (x, x₁, …, x_{dim X}) isolated in its fibre of D_{dim X}; (ii) Ξ ⊆ X′ for a proper Zariski closed X′ ⊊ X with deg X′ ≤ (deg_L X)^{2 dim X}.
hypotheses: X ⊆ A irreducible; Ξ ⊆ X°(ℚ̄).
proofSteps: If Stab(X) is positive-dimensional, X° = ∅; assume it is finite.
A tuple (x, x₁, …, x_{dim X}) is isolated iff 0 is an isolated point of (X − x) ∩ (X − x₁) ∩ ⋯ ∩ (X − x_{dim X}).

If (i) fails, there is a stage i₀ < dim X with W = (X − x) ∩ ⋯ ∩ (X − x_{i₀}) whose components C_j through 0 of dimension dim X − i₀ ≥ 1 persist after intersecting with X − y for every y ∈ Ξ; then Ξ ⊆ ⋃_j ⋂_{c ∈ C_j} (X − c).

Each ⋂_{c ∈ C_j}(X − c) is an intersection of at most dim X translates, proper since Stab(X) is finite; Bézout gives degree ≤ (deg X)^{dim X} and at most (deg X)^{dim X} components C_j, so deg X′ ≤ (deg_L X)^{2 dim X} (non-strict, source issue E13 of the GGK extraction).

sources.locator: Proposition A.3 and proof, pp. 228–229 (citing Rémond, Décompte, Proposition 3.3)
sources.match: Shows that either suitable points give isolated tuples or the set lies in a finite union of intersections of translates of X through positive-dimensional components, of degree bounded by Bézout.

acceptance: For X a curve (dim X = 1), alternative (ii) is Ξ ⊆ a finite set of at most (deg X)² points.
The bound on deg X′ is ≤, not <: E13 records the misprinted strict inequality.

nodes.title: Removing the height of X (GGK Lemma A.4)
nodes.statement: Let A ⊆ ℙⁿ be embedded by L as in Rémond’s inequalities and X ⊆ A irreducible of positive dimension. If S ⊆ X(ℚ̄) is finite and nonempty and every equidimensional subvariety Y ⊇ S of X of dimension dim X − 1 has deg_L Y > deg_L A·(deg_L X)²/g!, then h(X) ≤ (deg_L A/g! + 1)^{dim X+1} deg_L X (max_{x∈S} h(x) + 3 log(deg_L A/g!)).
hypotheses: S ⊆ X(ℚ̄) finite, not contained in any equidimensional codimension-one Y of degree ≤ deg_L A (deg_L X)²/g!.
dim X ≥ 1 and S is nonempty. Zero-dimensional X is handled separately in counting arguments.
proofSteps: The needed input is Rémond’s arithmetic interpolation lemma, restated as GGK Lemma A.4. Its low-degree containment hypothesis turns heights of a sufficiently spread finite set into the displayed bound for h(X).

Arithmetic Bézout alone does not prove this interpolation estimate, and hypersurfaces containing X cannot cut X down. A direct proof plan for the interpolation lemma is missing and remains an explicit gap; the lemma is not derived here from the qualitative Vojta method.

sources.locator: Lemma A.4, p. 229 (citing Rémond, Décompte, Lemma 3.1)
sources.match: Bounds the height of a subvariety by the heights of a finite set of its points that is not contained in any hypersurface section of small degree.

acceptance: For X a point use the separate identity h(X)=h(x); the positive-dimensional interpolation theorem is not applied to codimension −1.
The hypothesis on S cannot be dropped: if S lies in a low-degree hypersurface section, its points carry no information on the height of X.

nodes.title: Rémond’s bound for points of large height
nodes.statement: Let A, L be as in Rémond’s inequalities, X ⊆ A irreducible and Γ ⊆ A(ℚ̄) of finite rank. Assuming the counting theorem below for all subvarieties of dimension < dim X, there is c₆ = c₆(g, deg_L X, deg_L A) > 0 with #{P ∈ X°(ℚ̄) ∩ Γ : ĥ_L(P) ≥ c₅ max{1, h(X), h_Fal(A)}} ≤ c₆^{rk Γ + 1}. For curves (Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger Lemma 8.2): for C ⊆ A ⊆ ℙⁿ an irreducible curve that is not a translate of an algebraic subgroup, #{P ∈ C(ℚ̄) ∩ Γ : ĥ_L(P) > c·max{1, h(C), c_NT, h₁}} ≤ c^{rk Γ} with c = c(n, deg C).
hypotheses: L symmetric very ample projectively normal; X irreducible; Γ of finite rank.
proofSteps: Cover Γ_ℝ by at most ⌊(1 + (8c₄)^{1/2})^{rk Γ}⌋ cones on which ⟨P, Q⟩ ≥ (1 − 1/c₄)|P||Q|.

In one cone order the large points by norm P₀, P₁, …; for each j the block {P_{j+1}, …, P_{j+N′}} with N′ = (deg_L X)^{2g} c(g, (deg_L X)^{2g}, deg_L A)^{rk Γ+1} + 1 is not contained in a proper X′ of degree ≤ (deg_L X)^{2 dim X} (else the induction hypothesis on X′ contradicts the choice of N′).
The isolated-fibre alternative gives an isolated tuple with P_j; Rémond’s Mumford inequality then fails, so some P_k in the block has |P_k| > (1 + 1/c₄)|P_j|.

Choose M with (1 + 1/c₄)^M ≥ c₄; every M N′ steps the norm grows by c₄, so dim X + 1 such points satisfy Rémond’s Vojta hypotheses, contradicting the lower bound on |P₀|². Hence each cone holds fewer than (dim X)·M·N′ large points.

When the counting statement uses a non-strict large-height threshold, enlarge it beyond the upper bounds in the Vojta and Mumford alternatives (for example double their common positive constant). This avoids equality at the original threshold.

sources.locator: Appendix A.5, Step 1, (A.5)–(A.8) and proof, pp. 229–231
sources.match: Covers Γ ⊗ ℝ by boundedly many narrow cones; in each cone, blocks of consecutive large points escape small exceptional sets by induction, the isolated-fibre alternative and Rémond’s Mumford inequality force geometric norm growth, and Rémond’s Vojta inequality caps the number of growth steps.
States the curve case, citing Rémond’s Vojta and Mumford inequalities.
Records that the Vojta, Faltings and Bombieri proofs, refined by de Diego and Rémond, bound the number of points of large height.

acceptance: For rk Γ = 0 there are no points of positive height, so the bound is trivial.
The bound is exponential in rk Γ with base depending only on g and the degrees, not on the heights of A or X.

nodes.title: The packing hypothesis (Hyp pack)
nodes.statement: For (A, L) with L symmetric ample, X ⊆ A irreducible and Γ ⊆ A(ℚ̄) of finite rank, (Hyp pack) holds with constant c₀ = c₀(g, deg_L X) > 0 if for every P₀ ∈ X(ℚ̄): #{P − P₀ ∈ (X°(ℚ̄) − P₀) ∩ Γ : ĥ_L(P − P₀) ≤ c₀^{-1} max{1, h_Fal(A)}} ≤ c₀^{rk Γ + 1}.
hypotheses: (A, L), X, Γ as stated.
proofSteps: A predicate on the data; it is the input Rémond’s counting needs for the small points and the output of the gap principle.

sources.match: Formulates the hypothesis that around every base point few points of the subgroup on the complement of the Ueno locus are close in Néron–Tate distance, at the scale of the Faltings height.

acceptance: For Γ = A_tors (rank 0) the hypothesis says #((X° − P₀) ∩ A_tors) ≤ c₀ for every P₀: a uniform Manin–Mumford statement.
If X° = ∅ the hypothesis holds trivially.
With X° replaced by X, the hypothesis fails for X containing a positive-dimensional abelian subvariety B and Γ ⊇ B_tors: infinitely many torsion points of B are at distance 0.

uses.how: Rémond’s method under (Hyp pack) bounds #X° ∩ Γ
(Hyp pack) holds for L ⊗ [−1]^*L by the gap principle

api.name: PackingHypothesis
api.statement: The proposition (Hyp pack) for (A, L, X, Γ, c₀).

api.name: PackingHypothesis.mono_const
api.statement: If it holds with c₀ then it holds with every c₀′ ≥ c₀.

api.name: PackingHypothesis.subgroup
api.statement: If it holds for Γ with constant c₀, it holds with the same c₀ for every subgroup Γ′ ⊆ Γ of the same rank.

api.name: PackingHypothesis.translate
api.statement: Replacing X by X − Q and Γ by ⟨Γ, Q⟩ preserves the hypothesis with rank increased by at most one.

tests.name: PackingHypothesis.rank_zero_torsion
tests.statement: For Γ = A_tors (rank 0) the hypothesis says #((X° − P₀) ∩ A_tors) ≤ c₀ for every P₀: a uniform Manin–Mumford statement.

tests.name: PackingHypothesis.empty_ueno
tests.statement: If X° = ∅ the hypothesis holds trivially.

tests.name: PackingHypothesis.fails_without_ueno
tests.statement: With X° replaced by X, the hypothesis fails for X containing a positive-dimensional abelian subvariety B and Γ ⊇ B_tors: infinitely many torsion points of B are at distance 0.

nodes.title: Rémond’s counting theorem under (Hyp pack) (GGK Theorem 7.1)
nodes.statement: Assume (Hyp pack) holds for every (A, L), X, Γ with X generating A (in all dimensions up to that of the variety counted). Then for every polarized (A, L) over ℚ̄ with L symmetric and very ample, every irreducible X ⊆ A and every finite-rank Γ ⊆ A(ℚ̄): #(X°(ℚ̄) ∩ Γ) ≤ c(g, deg_L X, deg_L A)^{rk Γ + 1}, with c increasing in each argument.
hypotheses: (Hyp pack) for all generating subvarieties in dimensions ≤ dim X; L symmetric very ample.
proofSteps: The parent’s qualitative finite-rank Mordell–Lang theorem makes X°∩Γ finite: in its finite coset decomposition, every positive-dimensional coset is removed by the Ueno locus. Thus the minima over point configurations in the subsequent packing alternative are attained. This qualitative input does not use the uniform count being proved.
Reduce to X generating A: X ⊆ A′ + Q with A′ = ⟨X − X⟩, replace Γ by ⟨Γ, Q⟩ (rank + 1) and use (X − Q)° = X° − Q; deg_L A′ is bounded in g and deg_L X (GGK Lemma 2.5); then square the constant.
Induct on dim X. Step 1: the large-points bound.

Step 2 (removing h(X)): with c₇ = deg_L A (deg_L X)²/g! · c(g, deg_L A (deg_L X)²/g!, deg_L A) and N″ = c₇^{rk Γ+1} + 1, for pairwise distinct P₀, …, P_{N″} ∈ X° ∩ Γ, Lemma A.4 applied to X − P₀ bounds the number of P with ĥ(P − P₀) ≥ c₈² max_i ĥ(P_i − P₀) + c₉ max{1, h_Fal(A)} by c₁₀^{rk Γ+1}.

Step 3 (packing alternative): either #X° ∩ Γ ≤ N″(8c₈ + 1)^{rk Γ} + c₁₀^{rk Γ+1} (the factor is 8c₈ + 1, source issue E11), or some Q ∈ X° ∩ Γ has at most c₁₀^{rk Γ+1} points P with ĥ(P − Q) ≥ 2c₉ max{1, h_Fal(A)}.

Step 4: in the second case cover the ball of radius (2c₉ max{1, h_Fal})^{1/2} around Q by (1 + 2(2c₉c₀)^{1/2})^{rk Γ} balls of radius (c₀^{-1} max{1, h_Fal})^{1/2} (ball packing); each contains at most c₀^{rk Γ+1} points by (Hyp pack) (source issue E9: the ball count is c₀^{rk Γ+1}, not c₀).

sources.locator: Theorem 7.1, p. 220; proof sketch pp. 220–221; full proof Appendix A.5, Steps 1–4, pp. 229–232
sources.match: Proves the exponential count from the packing hypothesis by Rémond’s method: reduction to generating X, large points by the Vojta and Mumford inequalities, removal of h(X) by a finite set of points, and a packing alternative with a minimal radius.

acceptance: For rk Γ = 0 and Γ = A_tors this is a uniform Manin–Mumford count given (Hyp pack) at rank 0.
Without (Hyp pack) the method bounds only the large points; the small points are exactly what the gap principle controls.

nodes.title: (Hyp pack) holds for L ⊗ [−1]^*L (GGK Proposition 7.2)
nodes.statement: For an abelian variety A of dimension g over ℚ̄ with ample L, (Hyp pack) holds, with L replaced by L ⊗ [−1]^*L and a constant c₀ = c₀(g, deg_L X), for every irreducible X ⊆ A generating A and every finite-rank Γ ⊆ A(ℚ̄).
hypotheses: A abelian over ℚ̄, L ample; X irreducible generating A; Γ of finite rank.
proofSteps: Fix P₀ ∈ X(ℚ̄); apply the new gap principle to X − P₀ (which generates A): the points P − P₀ ∈ (X° − P₀) ∩ Γ with ĥ ≤ c₁ max{1, h_Fal(A)} lie in a proper X′ of degree < c₂.

Each component X† of X′ lies in a translate A† + Q of the abelian subvariety it generates; with Γ† = ⟨Γ, Q⟩ ∩ A†, Rémond’s counting (applicable by induction on dimension) bounds #((X† − Q)° ∩ Γ†) by c^{rk Γ+2}.
Use (X′)° ⊇ X° ∩ X′ and sum over the boundedly many components; set c₀ = max{c₁^{-1}, c₃} (source issue E10: c₁ enters inverted).

sources.match: Proves the packing hypothesis by induction on dim X: the gap principle applied to X − P₀ puts the close points in a bounded-degree exceptional set, whose components lie in translates of abelian subvarieties to which the induction and Rémond’s counting apply.

acceptance: The polarization L ⊗ [−1]^*L is symmetric; the gap principle is stated for it.
The constant depends only on g and deg_L X.

nodes.title: Rémond’s bound for one subvariety (David–Philippon form)
nodes.statement: For a subvariety X of an abelian variety A over ℚ̄ of dimension g with symmetric ample L, and a subgroup Γ ⊆ A(ℚ̄) of finite rank r, X(ℚ̄) ∩ Γ is a union of at most (2^{34} h₀(A) deg_L X)^{(r+1) g^5 (dim X + 1)²} sets (x_i + B_i)(ℚ̄) ∩ Γ with x_i + B_i ⊆ X and B_i abelian subvarieties, where h₀(A) = max{1, h(A)} for David–Philippon’s height of the embedded A.
hypotheses: A, L, X, Γ as stated.
proofSteps: Large points: the large-points bound (Rémond’s Vojta and Mumford inequalities), with c_NT and h₁ bounded by h₀(A).

Small points: David–Philippon’s lower bound for the Néron–Tate height on the complement of the Ueno locus in terms of h₀(A) and the degrees, combined with ball packing in the Néron–Tate space, bounds the points of height below the large-point threshold.

Induction on dim X handles the exceptional subvarieties; David–Philippon p. 643 records the resulting explicit constant. The David–Philippon article itself was not read for this plan (gap recorded): DGH and GGK quote only its form, and the explicit exponent is taken from the reviewed DGH extraction (item 67), whose reviewer read David–Philippon p. 643.

sources.locator: Proofs of Theorems 1.1 and 1.2, pp. 34–36 (arXiv v3), citing David–Philippon, Comment. Math. Helv. 77 (2002), p. 643
sources.match: Uses Rémond’s explicit bound for the number of cosets covering the points of a finite-rank subgroup on a fixed subvariety, in David–Philippon’s formulation, for the finitely many curves of small modular height.
Recalls the David–Philippon formulation of Rémond’s theorem, in which the small-point count enters as a hypothesis.

acceptance: The bound depends on the height of A, unlike the uniform theorems; it is the input for the finitely many curves of small modular height in DGH Theorem 1.1.
For r = 0 it is a bound, uniform in the base point, on torsion cosets: this repairs the small-height step of DGH Theorem 1.4 (source issue E6 of the DGH extraction).

nodes.title: The uniform count off the Ueno locus over ℚ̄
nodes.statement: For all g, d ≥ 0 there is c(g, d) > 0 such that for every abelian variety A over ℚ̄ of dimension g with ample L, every irreducible closed X ⊆ A with deg_L X = d and every finite-rank Γ ⊆ A(ℚ̄): #(X°(ℚ̄) ∩ Γ) ≤ c(g, d)^{1 + rk Γ}.
hypotheses: A abelian over ℚ̄, L ample; X irreducible closed; Γ of finite rank.
proofSteps: Replace L by (L ⊗ [−1]^*L)^{⊗4}, symmetric, very ample and projectively normal; degrees change by a factor depending only on g and dim X.
Reduce to X generating A: X ⊆ A′ + Q with A′ = ⟨X − X⟩ of degree bounded in g, d (GGK Lemma 2.5); pass to X − Q ⊆ A′ and ⟨Γ, Q⟩ ∩ A′, raising the rank by at most one.
For generating X, (Hyp pack) holds (GGK Proposition 7.2), so Rémond’s counting theorem gives the bound with deg_L A bounded in terms of g and d.

sources.match: Proves Theorem 1.1′ over ℚ̄: reduce to X generating A, then combine the packing hypothesis for L ⊗ [−1]^*L with Rémond’s counting theorem.

acceptance: For Γ = A_tors (rank 0) this is uniform Manin–Mumford: #(X° ∩ A_tors) ≤ c(g, d).
For X = A, X° = ∅ (for g ≥ 1) and the bound is vacuous.

nodes.title: Masser’s specialization of subgroups and endomorphisms
nodes.statement: Let 𝒜 → V be an abelian scheme over an irreducible variety V over ℚ̄ with generic fibre A over the function field, and Γ ⊆ A a finitely generated subgroup of sections. The set of v ∈ V(ℚ̄) at which the specialization Γ → Γ_v is injective and End(A_{K̄}) → End(𝒜_v) is an isomorphism is Zariski dense in V.
hypotheses: V irreducible over ℚ̄; 𝒜 → V abelian scheme; Γ finitely generated.

K is the generic function field. All data descend to a finitely generated model over a number field; after a finite cover, generators of the geometric generic endomorphism ring extend, so the displayed specialization map is defined.
proofSteps: Injectivity on Γ: Masser’s Main Theorem (1989) gives a dense set of specializations injective on a finitely generated group of sections (a quantitative Silverman specialization; the parent’s Kummer–Hilbert specialization in RP.5 gives injectivity on a dense set as well).

Masser 1996 bounds the exceptional endomorphism-specialization locus, while Masser 1989 supplies quantitative injectivity on Γ. To obtain simultaneous density one needs a common bounded-degree/height counting family in which the union of both exceptional sets is smaller than the family. Intersecting two Zariski-dense sets is insufficient; neither the separate density statements nor Hilbert irreducibility without a thinness theorem proves the joint assertion.
The simultaneous quantitative specialization argument has not been verified from Masser 1989. GGK §7.2 invokes it; the existing source gap is strengthened to record this precise closure obstruction.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 7.3, p. 224 (citing Masser, Trans. Amer. Math. Soc. 311 (1989), Main Theorem and Scholium 1; Masser, Bull. Soc. Math. France 124 (1996), Main Theorem)
sources.match: Uses Masser’s theorems that injectivity on a finitely generated group of sections and preservation of the endomorphism ring hold on a Zariski dense set of specializations.

For A over the function field of a variety V over a number field, the points of V(ℚ̄) of degree ≤ d and height ≤ h at which the absolute endomorphism ring of the fibre is not isomorphic to that of A lie on a hypersurface section of V of degree polynomial in max{d, h}.

acceptance: For a constant family with Γ generated by constant sections, the geometric endomorphism ring and Γ specialize identically at every point. Constancy of the abelian scheme alone does not make arbitrary sections constant.

For the Legendre family and Γ generated by a non-torsion section, specialization at a parameter where the section becomes torsion is not injective; such parameters are Zariski dense yet the good set is still dense.

nodes.title: Good models: the Ueno locus specializes
nodes.statement: Let X be a closed subvariety of an abelian variety A over the function field of an irreducible variety V over ℚ̄, spread out to a flat family 𝔛 ⊆ 𝒜 → V. After replacing V by a dense open, 𝔛 can be chosen so that for every v ∈ V(ℚ̄) the Ueno locus of 𝔛_v is the specialization of the Ueno locus of X; hence 𝔛_v° is the specialization of X°, and deg_L X = deg_{L_v} 𝔛_v.
hypotheses: V irreducible over ℚ̄; X ⊆ A over ℚ̄(V).
proofSteps: The maximal cosets in X have finitely many directions B of bounded degree (parent RP.5, Ueno locus, Rémond’s bounds); spread each B and the loci X_B with Z(X) = ⋃ (X_B + B) over a dense open.

A coset in a fibre 𝔛_v of dimension > 0 has a direction of bounded degree; the bounded-degree abelian subschemes of 𝒜 are finite étale over a dense open (parent RP.5, §5.13c), so after shrinking V every such direction is the specialization of a generic one, and the coset lies in the specialization of Z(X).
Degrees are constant in flat families.

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 7.3, p. 224 (citing Mazur, Bull. AMS 2000, pp. 219–220, and Hindry, Invent. Math. 94 (1988), Appendix 1, Lemma A)
sources.match: Chooses a good model in which the Ueno locus of each fibre is the specialization of the generic Ueno locus, so that the complements correspond and degrees are preserved by flatness.

acceptance: For X a curve of genus ≥ 2 the Ueno locus is empty generically and in every fibre of a good model.

A good model must control specialization of the given X and its Ueno locus after shrinking. Extra endomorphisms alone need not create cosets in X; avoiding all CM fibres by one Zariski-open restriction is not asserted.

nodes.title: From ℚ̄ to arbitrary fields for finitely generated subgroups (GGK Lemma 7.3)
nodes.statement: If the uniform count off the Ueno locus holds over ℚ̄, then for every algebraically closed field F of characteristic 0, every abelian variety A over F with ample L, every irreducible X ⊆ A and every finitely generated Γ ⊆ A(F) of rank ρ, #(X°(F) ∩ Γ) ≤ c(g, deg_L X)^{1+ρ} with the same function c.
hypotheses: F algebraically closed of characteristic 0; Γ finitely generated.
proofSteps: Choose a finitely generated ℚ̄-algebra over which A, L, X, the generators γ₁, …, γ_r of Γ and End(A) are defined; spread out over a regular irreducible variety V with A → V abelian, L relatively ample, endomorphisms extending, X flat, and γ_i sections.
Shrink V to make the model good for the Ueno locus.
For v in Masser’s dense set Θ, Γ → Γ_v is injective, so #(X°(F) ∩ Γ) ≤ #(𝔛_v°(ℚ̄) ∩ Γ_v) ≤ c(g, deg X)^{1 + rk Γ_v} ≤ c(g, deg X)^{1+ρ}.

sources.match: Spreads the data over a regular variety over ℚ̄ and specializes at a point of Masser’s dense set, where the subgroup injects and the Ueno locus specializes.

acceptance: For F = ℚ̄ the lemma is the identity.
Only finitely generated Γ are treated here; finite rank is reached by a filtered union.

nodes.title: The uniform count off the Ueno locus (GGK Theorem 1.1′)
nodes.statement: For all g, d ≥ 0 there is c(g, d) > 0 such that for every algebraically closed field F of characteristic 0, every abelian variety A over F of dimension g with ample L, every irreducible closed X ⊆ A with deg_L X = d and every subgroup Γ ⊆ A(F) of finite rank: #(X°(F) ∩ Γ) ≤ c(g, d)^{1 + rk Γ}.
hypotheses: F algebraically closed of characteristic 0; Γ of finite rank ρ.
proofSteps: Choose a finitely generated Γ₀ ⊆ A(F) of rank ρ with Γ contained in its division hull {x : [N]x ∈ Γ₀ for some N} (parent RP.5, finite rank).
For n ≥ 1, (1/n)Γ₀ = {x : [n]x ∈ Γ₀} is finitely generated of rank ρ; the specialization lemma gives #(X°(F) ∩ (1/n)Γ₀) ≤ c^{1+ρ} independently of n.

The (1/n!)Γ₀ form a filtered system exhausting the division hull, so #(X°(F) ∩ Γ) ≤ c^{1+ρ}. No End(A)-stability of Γ₀ is needed (source issue E14 of the GGK extraction: the printed choice Γ₀ = End(A)·Γ₀ can change the rank and is dropped).

sources.match: States the uniform count on the complement of the Ueno locus and proves it over arbitrary F from the finitely generated case by a filtered union of division groups.

acceptance: For Γ = 0, X°(F) ∩ Γ is empty or the origin, and the bound holds trivially.
The bound is independent of F and of A.

planet.name: Uniform count off the Ueno locus

nodes.title: From the count off the Ueno locus to Mordell–Lang (GGK Lemma 7.4)
nodes.statement: If the uniform count off the Ueno locus holds for all (A, L), X and Γ, then the uniform Mordell–Lang theorem holds: for X generating A, X(F) ∩ Γ is covered by at most c₄c₆^{1+rk Γ} + #(X°(F) ∩ Γ) cosets x + B ⊆ X, with c₄, c₆ depending only on dim A and deg_L X.
hypotheses: the uniform count off the Ueno locus for all data.
proofSteps: Reduce to X generating A as for the count over ℚ̄.

The maximal positive-dimensional directions B with x + B ⊆ X form a set Σ(X; A) of bounded size and degree (parent RP.5, Ueno locus: Bogomolov and Rémond’s bounds), and Z(X) = ⋃_B (X_B + B) with X_B = ⋂_{b∈B}(X − b) ∩ B^⊥ for a complement B^⊥ of bounded degree (parent RP.5, orthogonal complements; GGK cites Masser–Wüstholz for the complement).

Each coset of X ∩ Γ in direction B can be represented by a point of X_B° up to the addition isogeny f : B × B^⊥ → A: use the projected group Γ_B = pr₂(f^{-1}Γ) ⊆ B^⊥(F), of rank ≤ rk Γ (source issue E15 of the GGK extraction: the printed proof asks the representatives to lie in Γ itself).
Apply the count off the Ueno locus to each component of X_B with Γ_B, and once more to X° ∩ Γ for the zero-dimensional cosets.

sources.match: Writes the Ueno locus as a union over finitely many maximal coset directions B of X_B + B with X_B of bounded degree, chooses coset representatives off the Ueno loci of the X_B, and bounds their number by the count off the Ueno locus.

acceptance: If X° = X (no positive-dimensional cosets), the cosets are points and the statement is the count itself.
Γ_B is not Γ ∩ B^⊥: intersecting with Γ can lose the coset representatives (E15).

nodes.title: The uniform Mordell–Lang theorem (Gao–Ge–Kühne Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: For all integers g, d ≥ 0 there is c(g, d) > 0 such that for every algebraically closed field F of characteristic 0, every abelian variety A over F of dimension g with ample L, every irreducible closed X ⊆ A with deg_L X = d and every subgroup Γ ⊆ A(F) of finite rank, there are cosets x_i + B_i ⊆ X, 1 ≤ i ≤ N ≤ c(g, d)^{1 + rk Γ}, with X(F) ∩ Γ = ⋃_i (x_i + B_i)(F) ∩ Γ.
hypotheses: F algebraically closed of characteristic 0; L ample; X irreducible closed; Γ of finite rank.
proofSteps: Apply the Ueno reduction to the uniform count off the Ueno locus; reduce a non-generating X to the abelian subvariety it generates after translation, which increases the rank by at most one and changes the constant only in terms of g and d.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.1 and (1.1), p. 190; deduced from Theorem 1.1′ by Lemma 7.4, pp. 225–226
sources.match: States the uniform Mordell–Lang conjecture: the points of a finite-rank subgroup on a subvariety are covered by a number of cosets inside the subvariety bounded exponentially in the rank, with base depending only on the dimension and degree.

acceptance: For a curve C of genus ≥ 2 in its Jacobian this recovers the Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger–Kühne bound #(C(F) ∩ Γ) ≤ c(g)^{1 + rk Γ}.
For Γ = A_tors it gives uniform Manin–Mumford: the torsion points of X lie on at most c(g, d) torsion cosets in X.
The qualitative Mordell–Lang theorem of the parent (RP.5) is the statement without the bound on N; the uniform proof uses from it only the structure of the Ueno locus.

nodes.title: Uniform Mordell–Lang for curves (Kühne Theorem 4)
nodes.statement: For each g ≥ 2 there is c(g) > 0 such that for every smooth projective curve C of genus g over an algebraically closed field F of characteristic 0, every divisor D of degree 1 on C and every subgroup Γ ⊆ Jac(C)(F) of finite rank ρ, #(ι_D(C) ∩ Γ) ≤ c(g)^{1+ρ}. In particular a curve C of genus g over a number field K satisfies #C(K) ≤ c(g)^{1 + rk Jac(C)(K)}.
hypotheses: g ≥ 2; C smooth projective over F algebraically closed of characteristic 0; D of degree 1; Γ of finite rank.
proofSteps: ι_D(C) ⊆ Jac(C) is an irreducible curve of degree g for the theta polarization with ι_D(C)° = ι_D(C).
Apply the uniform count with (g, d) = (g, g).
For rational points over K, choose D = a rational point if one exists (otherwise C(K) = ∅) and Γ = Jac(C)(K), of rank rk Jac(C)(K) (Mordell–Weil, parent RP.1).

sources.match: States the uniform bound for points of a finite-rank subgroup on a curve embedded in its Jacobian, and the resulting bound for rational points depending only on the genus and the Mordell–Weil rank.
Recalls this bound as Kühne’s Theorem 4, obtained from the large-height bound and the gap principle, answering Mazur’s question.

acceptance: Γ = Jac(C)_tors recovers uniform Manin–Mumford for curves.
The bound for #C(K) does not depend on [K : ℚ], unlike Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger Theorem 1.1.

nodes.title: Counting on curves of large modular height (DGH Proposition 8.1)
nodes.statement: With M_g, τ, 𝔄_g and M as in the Abel–Jacobi bounds, there are c₁ ≥ 0 and c₂ ≥ 1 such that for every s ∈ M_g(ℚ̄) with h_{A_g,M}(τ(s)) ≥ c₁, every finite-rank Γ ⊆ 𝔄_{g,τ(s)}(ℚ̄) of rank ρ and every P₀ ∈ C_s(ℚ̄): #((C_s(ℚ̄) − P₀) ∩ Γ) ≤ c₂^{1+ρ}.
hypotheses: s with large modular height; Γ of finite rank; P₀ ∈ C_s.
proofSteps: Choose P_s as in the Abel–Jacobi bounds, so h(C_s − P_s) ≤ c max{1, h(τ(s))}; replace Γ by Γ′ = ⟨Γ, P₀ − P_s⟩, of rank ≤ ρ + 1.
Large points: Rémond’s bound (curve case of the large-points bound) with c_NT, h₁ ≤ c max{1, h(τ(s))}: at most c^{ρ+1} points have ĥ > c₀ max{1, h(τ(s))}.

Small points: they lie in a ball of radius (c₀ max{1, h})^{1/2}; cover it by (1 + 2(c₀c₃)^{1/2})^{ρ+1} balls of radius (max{1, h}/c₃)^{1/2} centred at points of the set (ball packing; source issue E13 of the DGH extraction fixes the printed count); each ball holds fewer than c₄ points or its centre lies in the bounded exceptional set Ξ_s (the Néron–Tate distance proposition).

sources.match: Counts large points by Rémond’s large-point lemma with the constants c_NT, h₁ and the curve height bounded linearly in the modular height, and small points by ball packing at radius comparable to the modular height together with the Néron–Tate distance proposition; a general base point is handled by enlarging Γ.

acceptance: The bound does not depend on the height of the curve once that height is large.
Below the threshold c₁ the proposition gives nothing; the small-height curves are handled by Northcott and Rémond’s single bound.

nodes.title: Uniform Mordell–Lang for curves of large modular height (DGH Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3)
nodes.statement: For g ≥ 2 and an immersion ι of the coarse moduli space A_{g,1} into ℙ^m over ℚ̄ there are c₁ = c₁(g, ι) ≥ 0 and c₂ = c₂(g, ι) ≥ 1 such that for every smooth curve C of genus g over ℚ̄, P₀ ∈ C(ℚ̄) and finite-rank Γ ⊆ Jac(C)(ℚ̄) of rank ρ with h(ι([Jac(C)])) ≥ c₁: #((C(ℚ̄) − P₀) ∩ Γ) ≤ c₂^{1+ρ}. In particular (Γ = Jac(C)_tors) #((C(ℚ̄) − P₀) ∩ Jac(C)_tors) ≤ c₂.
hypotheses: g ≥ 2; ι an immersion of the coarse moduli space; Jacobians of large height.
proofSteps: Choose a level-ℓ structure on C over ℚ̄, giving s ∈ M_g with τ(s) ↦ [Jac(C)] under the finite forgetful map ρ : A_{g,ℓ} → A_{g,1}.

Compare heights along ρ: h(ι(ρ(t))) ≤ c′h_{A_g,M}(t) + c″ (height machine; source issue E4 of the DGH extraction fixes the cross-reference), so a large height of ι([Jac(C)]) forces large modular height.
Apply the count for curves of large modular height; Γ = Jac(C)_tors has rank 0.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.2 and Corollary 1.3, p. 3; proof §8, pp. 35–36 (arXiv v3)
sources.match: States the bound for curves whose Jacobian has large height in a projective embedding of the coarse moduli space, and the torsion case as a corollary, deducing both from the count for curves of large modular height and a comparison of heights between the fine and coarse moduli spaces.

acceptance: Corollary 1.3 is the case ρ = 0.
The constants depend on the immersion ι, which the uniform Mordell–Lang theorem for curves removes together with the large-height hypothesis.

nodes.title: Finitely many curves of small modular height and bounded degree
nodes.statement: Fix g ≥ 2, d ≥ 1 and c₁. The smooth genus-g curves C defined over a number field F with [F : ℚ] ≤ d and h_{A_g,M}(τ(s)) < c₁ (for a level structure s over F′ ⊇ F) lie in finitely many ℚ̄-isomorphism classes, and the degree [F′ : F] of the field over which a level structure is defined is bounded in terms of g and the level.
hypotheses: [F : ℚ] ≤ d; modular height < c₁.
proofSteps: A level-ℓ structure is defined over an extension F′ of degree at most #GL_{2g}(ℤ/ℓ); so τ(s) has bounded degree and bounded height.
Northcott on the moduli space (ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeights R35.5) leaves finitely many τ(s); Torelli has finite fibres (StableReductionPartII MC.6), so finitely many s.
Each s determines C over ℚ̄ up to isomorphism (the paper says F′-isomorphism classes; ℚ̄-isomorphism is what is used).

sources.match: Shows by Northcott on the moduli space and finiteness of the Torelli map that the curves of bounded degree and small modular height fall into finitely many isomorphism classes over the algebraic closure.

acceptance: The field-degree bound is essential for Northcott: algebraic points of unbounded degree can have height zero (roots of unity in ℙ¹). Twists do not give distinct ℚ̄-isomorphism classes, so they are not a counterexample to this geometric finiteness statement.
The finite set depends on (g, d, c₁, ℓ).

nodes.title: Uniform bound for rational points (Dimitrov–Gao–Habegger Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: For integers g ≥ 2 and d ≥ 1 there is c = c(g, d) ≥ 1 such that every smooth geometrically irreducible projective curve C of genus g over a number field F with [F : ℚ] ≤ d satisfies #C(F) ≤ c^{1+ρ}, ρ = rk Jac(C)(F). The constant can be chosen to grow at most polynomially in d.
proofSteps: If C(F) = ∅ there is nothing to prove; otherwise take P₀ ∈ C(F) and Γ = Jac(C)(F), of rank ρ (Mordell–Weil, parent RP.1).
Large modular height: the count for curves of large modular height.
Small modular height: finitely many curves over ℚ̄; for each, Rémond’s single bound (David–Philippon form) gives a bound uniform in P₀ and exponential in ρ.

Polynomial growth in d: in the small-height case h_Fal and the David–Philippon height are bounded (ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeights R35.5), and Rémond’s bound is polynomial in D·max{1, h_DP} with D ≤ [F′ : F]d.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.1 and (1.1), pp. 1–2; proof §8 and the remark after it, pp. 34–35 (arXiv v3)
sources.match: Answers Mazur’s question for curves of bounded degree: large modular height by the count for curves of large height, small modular height by Northcott and Rémond’s bound for each of finitely many curves, with polynomial growth in the degree from the explicit form of Rémond’s bound and bounds for the Faltings and David–Philippon heights.

acceptance: The uniform Mordell–Lang theorem for curves removes the dependence on d.
For ρ = 0, #C(F) is bounded in terms of g and d only (torsion packets are bounded).

nodes.title: Canonical heights as heights of the invariant adelic extension
nodes.statement: Let k be a field and K a function field of one variable over k (or k = ℤ and K a number field), A an abelian variety over K, L a symmetric ample line bundle and L̄ its invariant adelic extension with [2]^*L̄ = 4L̄. For x ∈ A(K̄), h_{L̄}(x) = ĥ_L(x), the Néron–Tate height in the normalization of adelic heights (over K, residue degrees over k), and for a closed subvariety X ⊆ A_{K̄} of dimension d, h_{L̄}(X) = (L̄|_X)^{d+1}/((d+1) deg_L X) equals the canonical height ĥ_L(X) of X (the limit n^{-2}h([n]X), equivalently the model intersection under everywhere good reduction).
hypotheses: K a number field or a function field of one variable over k; L symmetric ample on A.
proofSteps: Both sides are invariant under [2] up to the factor 4 (L̄ by construction, AH.5; the canonical heights by the parent RP.0), and both differ from a model height by a bounded amount; Tate’s uniqueness gives equality on points.

For subvarieties, h_{L̄}(X) is the limit of model intersections along the Tate sequence 4^{-n}[2^n]^*L̄₀, which is the parent’s definition of ĥ_L(X) (model intersections agree with model metrics, RP.0); under everywhere good reduction it is the intersection of the rigidified symmetric model.

sources.match: Defines canonical heights of subvarieties over function fields as limits of normalized model intersection numbers under multiplication; the identification with adelic heights is not stated there and is derived in this node.

Uses the invariant adelic extension of a symmetric rigidified bundle on an abelian scheme (citing Yuan–Zhang Theorem 6.1.1), normalizes heights of points of adelic line bundles over global fields, and takes the Néron–Tate height as half the canonical height of the twice-theta bundle; the equality of the two heights is used without a displayed statement.

acceptance: For X a point the subvariety height is the point height.
For X = A (or an abelian subvariety, or a torsion translate of one) both sides vanish.
The normalization over function fields keeps k fixed: replacing K by a finite extension multiplies neither side (heights are divided by the extension degree).

nodes.title: Essential minimum and canonical height over function fields (Zhang, Gubler)
nodes.statement: Let K be a function field of one variable over an algebraically closed field k, A/K an abelian variety, L symmetric ample and X ⊆ A_{K̄} closed and irreducible of dimension d. With e₁(X) = sup_{U ⊆ X open dense} inf_{x ∈ U(K̄)} ĥ_L(x): e₁(X) ≥ ĥ_L(X) ≥ e₁(X)/(d + 1). In particular ĥ_L(X) = 0 if and only if X contains a dense set of small points (X(ε) Zariski dense for every ε > 0).
hypotheses: K/k of transcendence degree 1 with k algebraically closed; X irreducible.
proofSteps: Apply the fundamental inequality of ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeightsPartII AH.4 to L̄|_X, which is nef with ample (hence big) geometric part, and identify h_{L̄}(X) with ĥ_L(X) and point heights with Néron–Tate heights (the adelic comparison).

Both inequalities are the Yuan–Zhang fundamental inequality (Theorem 5.3.3 and Lemma 5.3.4) as planned in AH.4; Xie–Yuan quote only the upper one (Zhang, Gubler Lemma 4.1) and Gao–Habegger only the equivalence (Gubler Corollary 4.4).

If X(ε) is dense for all ε then e₁(X) = 0, so ĥ_L(X) = 0; conversely ĥ_L(X) = 0 gives e₁(X) ≤ (d + 1)·0 = 0, i.e. dense small points. The converse direction is the one Xie–Yuan’s induction needs (source issue E3 of the XY extraction).

sources.locator: Proof of Lemma 5.2, p. 23 (arXiv v1), citing Zhang (1995, Theorem 1.10) and Gubler (2007, Lemma 4.1)
sources.match: Uses Zhang’s fundamental inequality in Gubler’s function-field form to show that dense small points force canonical height zero.

sources.locator: §A.3, p. 57 (arXiv v3), citing Zhang and Gubler (2007, Corollary 4.4)
sources.match: Uses the equivalence of vanishing essential minimum and vanishing canonical height of a subvariety over a function field.

acceptance: For X a point, e₁ = ĥ(x) = ĥ(X).
For X special (a torsion translate of the image of a constant subvariety), ĥ(X) = 0 and small points are dense.
Over a number field the same inequalities hold (parent RP.5 essential minimum); the statement here is the function-field version needed for the geometric Bogomolov conjecture.

nodes.title: Dense sets of small points over a function field
nodes.statement: Let k be algebraically closed, K/k finitely generated of transcendence degree ≥ 1 with a polarization (S, M) (S a normal projective model of K over k, M ample), A/K an abelian variety, L symmetric ample and ĥ the canonical height defined by L and (S, M). For a closed subvariety X ⊆ A_{K̄} and ε > 0 put X(ε) = {x ∈ X(K̄) : ĥ(x) < ε}. X contains a dense set of small points of A/K/k if X(ε) is Zariski dense in X for every ε > 0.
hypotheses: K/k finitely generated, trdeg ≥ 1, k algebraically closed; polarization (S, M).
proofSteps: Use the parent’s canonical heights over polarized function fields (RP.0).
Independence: two choices of (L, S, M) give heights with n^{-1}ĥ ≤ ĥ′ ≤ nĥ (comparison of ample bundles, parent RP.0 height laws), so density of X(ε) for all ε is unchanged.

sources.match: Defines the set of points of height below ε and the property of containing a dense set of small points, noting its independence of the choice of L and of the polarization since any two such heights bound each other up to positive multiples.

acceptance: A torsion point x has ĥ(x) = 0, so {x} has dense small points.
If A has trivial geometric K̄/k̄-trace, a non-torsion point has ĥ > 0 and {x} has no dense small points.
For a constant elliptic curve E₀ ⊗_k K and a point of E₀(k) of infinite order, ĥ = 0, so a non-torsion point can have dense small points over a function field (the trace).

uses.how: the hypothesis of the geometric Bogomolov conjecture
the conclusion is that small points are not dense

Non-torsion constant points then have geometric height zero. Ordinary trace zero cannot replace geometric trace zero.

nodes.title: Special subvarieties of an abelian variety over a function field
nodes.statement: Fix algebraic closures k̄ ⊆ K̄ for a function-field extension K/k, and let A/K be abelian. Let (T,tr) be the K̄/k̄-trace of A_{K̄}, with tr : T_{K̄} → A_{K̄}. An irreducible closed X ⊆ A_{K̄} is special for A/K/k if X = tr(Y_{K̄}) + (a+B), where Y ⊆ T is an irreducible closed subvariety over k̄, B ⊆ A_{K̄} is an abelian subvariety, and a is torsion. Here a torsion subvariety means one torsion translate, as in XY (1.5); a reducible closed set is treated componentwise.
hypotheses: K/k a function-field extension, fixed algebraic closures k̄ ⊆ K̄; A/K abelian; X geometrically irreducible over K̄.
proofSteps: Apply the parent’s Chow trace to the regular extension K̄/k̄. The trace map has finite kernel (a closed immersion in characteristic zero; possibly inseparable kernel in positive characteristic). Its image and the torsion translate are summed by the proper addition map.
A torsion subvariety is a torsion translate a + C of an abelian subvariety C (XY’s convention for (1.5)); the sum is the image of the addition map.

sources.match: Defines special subvarieties as sums of the trace image of a constant subvariety and a torsion subvariety, first for k algebraically closed and then, in (3.3), for k algebraically closed in K using algebraic closures.

acceptance: A point x ∈ A(K̄) is special iff x ∈ tr(T(k̄)) + A_tors.
For a constant abelian variety A = A₀ ⊗_k K and a curve C₀ ⊆ A₀, C₀ ⊗ K̄ is special though it is not a torsion subvariety.
A genus-≥ 2 curve in its Jacobian over K with J of trivial trace (a non-isotrivial curve with simple non-isotrivial Jacobian) is not special.

uses.how: the conclusion of the geometric Bogomolov conjecture
the field over which X becomes special is minimal and unique
over a curve, a subvariety dominating S is generically special iff its geometric generic fibre is special in this sense

api.statement: The predicate X special for A/K/k.

api.statement: Every torsion subvariety is special (Y = {0}).

api.statement: tr(Y ⊗ K̄) is special for every Y ⊆ T.

api.name: IsSpecial.trivial_trace

api.statement: For K = k(S) with S a curve over k = ℚ̄ (or algebraically closed of characteristic 0), an irreducible 𝒳 ⊆ 𝒜 dominating S is generically special (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuliPartII B2) iff its geometric generic fibre is special.

nodes.title: Special subvarieties have dense small points
nodes.statement: If X ⊆ A_{K̄} is special for A/K/k, then X(ε) is Zariski dense in X for every ε > 0.
hypotheses: X special.
proofSteps: Points of tr(Y ⊗ K̄)(k̄-rational, i.e. images of Y(k̄)) have height 0 (constant points are in the kernel of the Néron–Tate height over function fields, parent RP.1) and are dense in tr(Y ⊗ K̄).
Torsion points of an abelian subvariety C are dense in C (prime-to-p torsion is dense, AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A3) and have height 0.
Sums of height-zero points have height zero (ĥ is a quadratic form whose zero set is a subgroup); a dense subset of a product maps onto a dense subset of the sum.

sources.locator: §1.1, p. 3 (arXiv v1), citing Lang, Fundamentals of Diophantine Geometry, Chapter 6, Theorem 5.4
sources.match: Records that special subvarieties contain dense sets of small points, the easy direction of the geometric Bogomolov conjecture.

acceptance: A torsion point has dense small points trivially.
Over number fields the trace part is absent, and special means torsion subvariety.

nodes.title: The complement X* of the generically special subvarieties (GH Proposition 1.3)
nodes.statement: Let π : 𝒜 → S be an abelian scheme over a smooth irreducible curve S over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0 and X ⊆ 𝒜 irreducible closed. Only finitely many generically special subvarieties of 𝒜 contained in X are maximal for that property; X* = X ∖ ⋃{Y ⊆ X generically special} is Zariski open in X, and X* = ∅ if and only if X is generically special.
hypotheses: S smooth irreducible curve over algebraically closed k of characteristic 0; X ⊆ 𝒜 irreducible closed.
proofSteps: Split A_{K̄} up to isogeny as A′ × A″ with A′ = tr(A^{K/k} ⊗ K̄) and (A″)^{K/k} = 0 (Poincaré reducibility).

A generically special Y corresponds on the geometric generic fibre to a subvariety of V × A″ meeting V₀(k) × A″_tor densely, with V₀ = A^{K/k}; the special-points theorem gives the product form and finiteness of maximal ones.
X* is the complement of a finite union of closed subsets, hence open.

sources.locator: Definition 1.2 and display below it, p. 3; Proposition 1.3, p. 3; proof §3.1, p. 12 (arXiv v3)
sources.match: Defines generically special subvarieties and the complement X*, and proves finiteness of the maximal ones through the Poincaré splitting into trace part and trace-free part and the special-points theorem for V₀(k) × A_tor.

acceptance: For the image X of a torsion section, X is generically special and X* = ∅.
X = 𝒜 is generically special (B = A), so 𝒜* = ∅.
For a non-torsion section of a non-isotrivial elliptic surface, X* = X.

uses.how: the height inequality holds on X*
X ⊗ K̄ not special iff X* ≠ ∅ for its closure

nodes.title: Torsion of bounded degree has bounded order (GH Proposition B.1)
nodes.statement: Let S be a smooth irreducible quasi-projective variety over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0, K = k(S), and A an abelian variety over K with (A_{K̄})^{K̄/k} = 0. For every D ≥ 1 the orders of the points of {P ∈ A(K̄)_tors : [K(P) : K] ≤ D} are bounded in terms of A and D.
hypotheses: S smooth irreducible quasi-projective over algebraically closed k of characteristic zero; A is defined over K=k(S) and has trivial geometric K̄/k-trace.
proofSteps: Spread A to an abelian scheme over a dense open S° ⊆ S; the closure of a torsion point of order N is a component of 𝒜[N], finite étale over S°.
Finite étale covers of S° of degree ≤ D are finitely many up to isomorphism after fixing ramification (GH Lemma B.2: the compositum of all of them is a finite extension K_D).

All such torsion points lie in A(K_D)_tors, which is finite by Lang–Néron since the trace is zero (parent RP.1). The geometric trace hypothesis ensures the trace remains zero over the finite extension K_D.

sources.locator: Proposition B.1 and proof, p. 58; the case dim S = 1 is the claim (3.2), p. 14 (arXiv v3)
sources.match: Shows that the closure of a torsion point of bounded degree is finite étale over a dense open, bounds the compositum of the fields generated, and concludes by Lang–Néron.

acceptance: For a constant abelian variety (non-zero trace) the statement fails: all torsion of A₀(k) is K-rational.
D = 1 gives finiteness of A(K)_tors for trace-free A.

An isotrivial twist with zero ordinary K/k-trace can acquire all constant torsion over a fixed finite extension, giving bounded-degree torsion of unbounded order. The geometric trace hypothesis excludes it.

nodes.title: Special points of V₀(k) × A_tors (GH Propositions 3.1 and B.3)
nodes.statement: Let k be algebraically closed of characteristic 0, S a smooth irreducible quasi-projective variety over k, K = k(S)‾, A an abelian variety over K with A^{K/k} = 0, V₀ an irreducible variety over k, V = V₀ ⊗_k K and Σ = V₀(k) × A_tors. (i) If Y ⊆ V × A is irreducible closed with Y(K) ∩ Σ Zariski dense in Y, then Y = (W₀ ⊗_k K) × (P + B) with W₀ ⊆ V₀ irreducible closed, P ∈ A_tors and B an abelian subvariety. (ii) A given Y contains only finitely many maximal subvarieties of this form.
hypotheses: k algebraically closed, char 0; A over k(S)‾ of trivial trace; V₀ irreducible over k.
proofSteps: Choose a finitely generated function field of definition F/k and a smooth model over which the geometric abelian variety, Y, and the finite set of subgroup types are defined. Apply the bounded-degree torsion theorem to that field F and its finite extensions; degrees over the already algebraically closed K̄ would carry no information.

View Y as a family over V₀: for v ∈ V₀(k) the fibre Y_v ⊆ A meets A_tors densely only along torsion cosets; uniform Manin–Mumford in families (parent RP.5) gives finitely many directions B and a uniform bound on the number of cosets.

The torsion points involved have bounded degree over K by a Galois-orbit count (k-points of V₀ are Galois-fixed), hence bounded order by the bounded-order proposition; apply [N] ∘ (A → A/B) to reduce to B = 0 and a finite set of torsion points.

Fibre dimension then forces Y = (W₀ ⊗ K) × (P + B); finiteness of maximal ones follows from the finiteness of directions and of torsion orders. Misprints E1–E3 and the torsion-point convention E20 of the GH extraction are applied.

sources.locator: Proposition 3.1 and proof, pp. 12–15 (curve base); Proposition B.3, p. 59 (any base) (arXiv v3)
sources.match: Proves the product structure of subvarieties with dense special points using uniform Manin–Mumford in the family over V₀, a Galois-orbit bound and the bounded order of torsion of bounded degree, then extends from curves to bases of any dimension.

acceptance: For V₀ a point, (i) is Manin–Mumford over K for trace-free A.
Trivial trace is necessary: for constant A = A₀ ⊗ K, the diagonal of A₀ × A₀ meets V₀(k) × A_tors (V₀ = A₀) in a dense set without being a product.

nodes.title: Height inequality over a curve (Gao–Habegger Theorem 1.4)
nodes.statement: Let π : 𝒜 → S be an abelian scheme over a smooth irreducible curve S over ℚ̄, L a symmetric relatively ample line bundle and M ample on a compactification S̄. For every closed irreducible X ⊆ 𝒜 there is c > 0 with h_{S̄,M}(π(P)) ≤ c(1 + ĥ_{𝒜,L}(P)) for all P ∈ X*(ℚ̄). With L′ = L ⊗ π^*M and an immersion ι : 𝒜 → ℙ^m × S̄ by (L′)^{⊗n}, also h_{𝒜,L′}(P) ≤ c(1 + ĥ_{𝒜,L}(P)) on X*(ℚ̄) (Theorem 1.4′).
hypotheses: S smooth irreducible curve over ℚ̄; L symmetric relatively ample; M ample on S̄; X ⊆ 𝒜 closed irreducible.
proofSteps: If X is generically special, X* = ∅. Otherwise X is non-degenerate: over a curve, degenerate implies generically special (Gao–Habegger Theorem 5.1, AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuliPartII B2).
The height inequality for non-degenerate subvarieties gives a dense open U ⊆ X with ĥ(P) ≥ c₁h_{S̄,M}(π(P)) − c₂ on U, i.e. h(π(P)) ≤ c(1 + ĥ(P)).
Induct on dim X: the components Z_i of X ∖ U satisfy X* ⊆ U ∪ ⋃ Z_i* (GH (10.4)), and the induction hypothesis applies to each Z_i.

Theorem 1.4′: h_{𝒜,L′}(P) = n^{-1}h(ι(P)) + h_{S̄,M}(π(P)) up to O(1), and Silverman–Tate bounds n^{-1}h(ι(P)) by ĥ(P) + c(1 + h(π(P))) (the first inequality comes from the definition of L′, not from (1.1); source issue E15 of the GH extraction).

Gao–Habegger’s own proof of the inequality on a dense open (their §§6–10: auxiliary subvarieties, lattice points in Betti coordinates, many isolated division points, Habegger’s degree lemmas) is an alternative route, not used here.
If X is vertical over S, π(X) is one point, its base height is bounded, and the inequality follows from ĥ ≥ 0 after enlarging c. The generic-fibre argument is only needed for X dominating S.

sources.locator: Theorem 1.4 and (1.1), p. 4; Theorem 1.4′, p. 5; proof §10.2, p. 52 (arXiv v3)
sources.match: States the height inequality on the complement of the generically special subvarieties over a one-dimensional base and the version with a naive height, proving it by induction on dim X from the inequality on a dense open.
Generalizes the inequality to bases of any dimension for non-degenerate subvarieties.

acceptance: The inequality fails on torsion multisections: ĥ = 0 while h(π(P)) is unbounded, so X* cannot be enlarged to X.
For X = 𝒜 (generically special) the statement is empty.

nodes.title: Geometric Bogomolov over function fields of curves over ℚ̄ (Gao–Habegger Theorem 1.1)
nodes.statement: Let K be the function field of a smooth projective curve S over ℚ̄, A an abelian variety over K with symmetric ample L, and X ⊆ A irreducible closed with X ⊗_K K̄ irreducible and not special (not of the form B + (Z ⊗_ℚ̄ K̄) with Z ⊆ A^{K̄/ℚ̄} closed irreducible and B a torsion coset of A ⊗_K K̄). Then there is ε > 0 such that {x ∈ X(K̄) : ĥ_{K,A,L}(x) ≤ ε} is not Zariski dense in X.
hypotheses: K = ℚ̄(S), S smooth projective curve; X ⊗ K̄ irreducible and not special.
proofSteps: Spread A, L to π : 𝒜 → S° over a dense open and let 𝒳 be the closure of X; X ⊗ K̄ not special means 𝒳 is not generically special, so 𝒳* is open dense.
For x ∈ X(K̄) with σ_x(S′) meeting 𝒳*, the height inequality gives h_S(ρ(t)) ≤ c(1 + ĥ(σ_x(t))) for t ∈ S′ with σ_x(t) ∈ 𝒳*.
Silverman’s height limit (parent RP.0): ĥ(σ_x(t))/h_S(ρ(t)) → ĥ_{K,A}(x) as h_S(ρ(t)) → ∞; hence ĥ_{K,A}(x) ≥ 1/c, i.e. ≥ deg(S)/c in GH’s normalization.
Small points therefore lie in the closed complement of 𝒳* restricted to the generic fibre, a proper closed subset of X.

sources.match: Spreads out to an abelian scheme over an open of the curve, applies the height inequality to the closure of X and compares with Silverman’s height limit along the section of each small point, obtaining a lower bound for the function-field height off a proper closed subset.

acceptance: A special X has dense small points (special-has-small-points), so the hypothesis is necessary.
Agrees with Xie–Yuan Theorem 1.1 for characteristic 0 and transcendence degree 1.

nodes.title: The height inequality with Moriwaki heights (GH Theorem A.3)
nodes.statement: Let k₀ be finitely generated over ℚ with a polarization B, 𝒜 → S an abelian scheme over a smooth irreducible quasi-projective curve over k₀, L symmetric relatively ample and M ample on S̄ (both over k₀), and X ⊆ 𝒜 closed irreducible over k₀ with X* as in the generically special locus for k = k̄₀. There is c > 0 depending on B, 𝒜/S, X, L, M with h^B_{S̄,M}(π(P)) ≤ c(1 + ĥ^B_{𝒜,L}(P)) for all P ∈ X*(k̄₀).
hypotheses: k₀ finitely generated over ℚ with polarization B; S smooth irreducible curve over k₀.
proofSteps: Reduce to k₀ ⊆ ℂ by a field isomorphism (Moriwaki heights transport, AH.6).

Rerun the proof of the height inequality: the Betti-form and intersection arguments are geometric over ℂ; only the height machine, Néron–Tate heights and Silverman–Tate are replaced by their Moriwaki versions (ArakelovGeometryAndAbelianHeightsPartII AH.6).
The left-hand side is the base height h^B_{S̄,M}(π(P)) (E24).

sources.locator: Theorem A.3 and sketch, p. 56 (arXiv v3)
sources.match: States the height inequality over a curve over a finitely generated field with Moriwaki heights, obtained by repeating the proof with the Moriwaki height machine and Silverman–Tate; the printed left-hand side names the wrong height (source issue E24 of the GH extraction).

acceptance: For k₀ a number field, Moriwaki heights are Weil heights and the statement is the height inequality over a curve.
This is a sketch in the source; the plan treats it as a theorem whose proof is the same as over ℚ̄ with the AH.6 inputs.

nodes.title: Geometric Bogomolov over function fields of curves in characteristic zero
nodes.statement: Gao–Habegger’s Theorem 1.1 holds with ℚ̄ replaced by any algebraically closed field k of characteristic 0: for K the function field of a smooth projective curve over k, A/K abelian with symmetric ample L and X ⊆ A irreducible with X ⊗ K̄ irreducible and not special, the points of X(K̄) of small canonical height are not Zariski dense.
hypotheses: k algebraically closed of characteristic 0; S smooth projective curve over k.
proofSteps: Descend S, A, L, X to a finitely generated k₀ ⊆ k; with Moriwaki heights the height inequality and Silverman’s limit (AH.6) give, as over ℚ̄, that X has no dense small points over k̄₀(S), i.e. e₁(X_{k̄₀}) > 0. Choose a big Moriwaki polarization on k₀ so that the ample base height has the unboundedness needed in the specialization-limit argument; arbitrary degenerate polarizations need not supply it.

By the Zhang–Gubler inequalities, e₁ > 0 iff ĥ(X) > 0; the canonical height of a subvariety is unchanged by extending the algebraically closed constant field from k̄₀ to k (parent RP.0 base and constant extension).
Hence ĥ(X_k) > 0 and e₁(X_k) ≥ ĥ(X_k) > 0. The source calls this a sketch; the plan supplies the two inputs as nodes.

sources.match: Sketches the extension to all algebraically closed fields of characteristic 0: descend to a finitely generated field, run the proof with Moriwaki heights, and pass to the full constant field through the essential minimum.

acceptance: Contained in Xie–Yuan Theorem 1.1, which also covers positive characteristic and higher transcendence degree.
The constant field extension does not create new special structure: the trace does not grow under algebraically closed constant extension in characteristic 0.

nodes.title: Abelian varieties defined over a subfield up to isogeny
nodes.statement: Let K be a field, k ⊆ K a subfield and A an abelian variety over K. A is defined over k up to isogeny if there is an abelian variety A′ over k with A isogenous to A′ ⊗_k K.
hypotheses: k ⊆ K fields; A/K abelian.
proofSteps: A predicate on intermediate fields, using isogenies of abelian varieties over K (AbelianSchemesAndArithmeticModuli A6).

sources.match: Defines when an abelian variety over K is defined over a subfield up to isogeny.

acceptance: Every A is defined over K up to isogeny.
A₀ ⊗_k K is defined over k.
The Legendre elliptic curve y² = x(x − 1)(x − t) over k(t) (k algebraically closed) has non-constant j-invariant and is not defined over k up to isogeny.

uses.how: the set of algebraically closed intermediate fields over which A is defined up to isogeny has a least element k_A
the field k_{A,X} over which X becomes special contains k_A

api.statement: For a regular extension K/k (in particular for algebraically closed k), A is defined over k up to isogeny iff the K/k-trace map is an isogeny. No trace existence or base-change claim is made for arbitrary inseparable extensions.
